1.open: Think of a time you were welcomed somewhere you did not expect to be, like a family dinner, a team or a new home. What made you feel included?
questions: Paul says God "has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms" (v. 3). What do you think a spiritual blessing is, and how is it different from the blessings we usually ask God for?

Verse 4 says God "chose us in Him before the foundation of the world." Some people find that comforting, some confusing and some troubling. Which is it for you right now, and why? It is fine to say you are not sure.

Christians read "chose" and "predestined" (vv. 4, 5, 11) in different ways. Some think God chose particular people, some think God chose a people in Christ that anyone can join by faith, and some think God chose based on knowing who would believe. Whatever view you lean toward, what does this chapter make clear about where our salvation starts?

Paul says God planned "adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ" (v. 5). In Paul's day an adopted child received the family name and a full share of the inheritance. What would it mean to you to be welcomed into a family like that without earning it?

Verse 7 speaks of "redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses," and verse 8 says this grace was "lavished on us." Where do you find it hard to believe forgiveness is given generously and not handed out in small portions?

Verses 13 and 14 say believers were "sealed with the promised Holy Spirit," who is "the pledge of our inheritance." A pledge is a first payment that promises more to come. How does it change the way you see your life to think God has already put down that first payment?

Paul prays that "the eyes of your heart may be enlightened" so that we know God's hope and "the surpassing greatness of His power" (vv. 18, 19). What would you most like to see more clearly about God right now?
1.life: Paul starts with what God has already done before he says anything about what we should do. This week, each morning, name one thing you have received from God that you did not earn, and say thank you before you start your day.
1.prayer: Bless God together, as Paul does in verse 3, for what he has given in Christ. Then pray Paul's prayer for one another: that the eyes of your hearts would be opened to know his hope.
1.tip: Verses 4, 5 and 11 can pull the group into a long argument about choice and free will. Say up front that faithful Christians read these verses differently, then bring the group back to what all of them agree on: salvation begins with God's grace, and Paul writes it as praise, not as a puzzle.

2.open: Think of a time you felt like an outsider, then someone welcomed you in. What did they do that made the difference?
questions: Paul says, "you were dead in your trespasses and sins" (v. 1). Why do you think he uses such strong language? What does a person who is dead need?
Verses 4 and 5 turn on the words "But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy" (v. 4). What changes in the story at this point, and who does the work?

Verse 8 says, "it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God." How is a gift different from a wage? Where do you find it hard to simply receive?

Christians read this chapter a little differently on how faith and good works fit together in being saved. Verse 10 says we are "created in Christ Jesus to do good works." What do you take that to mean for how we live?

Paul reminds the non-Jewish readers that they were once "without hope and without God in the world" (v. 12). Why might it matter to remember where you started? If you honestly aren't sure where you stand with God, what would you say?
Verse 14 says Christ "has torn down the dividing wall of hostility." What walls between groups of people do you see today, in the church or outside it?
Verse 19 says you are "no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household." What would it look like for our group to feel like that to a newcomer?
2.life: This week, reach out to one person who might feel like an outsider, at church, work, school or in your neighborhood. Invite them for coffee or a meal, and simply listen.
2.prayer: Thank God for rescuing us by grace, as a gift and not a wage. Ask him to break down walls between people you know and to make your group a place where outsiders feel at home.
2.tip: Verses 8 to 10 can start a debate about faith and works, and Christians do land in different places. Say that plainly, then steer back to what everyone shares: salvation is God's gift, and good works flow from it. Keep room for anyone who feels they have not earned a place.

3.open: Think of a time you walked into a room where you didn't know anyone. What made you feel welcome, or what made you feel left out?
questions: Paul writes from prison, yet calls himself "the prisoner of Christ Jesus" (v. 1). Why might he describe his situation that way? How do you tend to describe the hard circumstances in your own life?

Paul says the Gentiles, meaning non-Jewish people, are "fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus" (v. 6). What would it have meant for non-Jewish readers to hear that they were full equals?
Who have you been taught, openly or quietly, to see as an outsider? What would change if they were treated as full family rather than guests?
Paul says he is "less than the least of all the saints," yet grace was given him to preach (v. 8). When have you been handed a task you felt unqualified for? What helped, or what would have helped?

Verse 10 says God's wisdom is made known "through the church." What does a church look like when people who are very different from each other belong together? Where have you seen that, or where is it missing?
Verse 12 says we may enter God's presence "with boldness and confidence." Does that feel true to you right now, or does God feel distant? Answer as honestly as you can, whichever way it is.
Paul prays that we would know a love "that surpasses knowledge" (v. 19). Where is it hardest for you to believe you are loved, and what might help you grasp it more?
3.life: Think of one person who is often on the edge of your circle at church, work, school or in your neighborhood. This week, invite them to a meal or a coffee, and simply listen.
3.prayer: Ask God to strengthen each person in the group inwardly, and to help everyone to be "rooted and grounded in love" (v. 17). Pray for any person or group your church has overlooked.
3.tip: Christians differ on whether the church in this chapter is something new alongside Israel or the widening and fulfillment of Israel itself. Say that in one line and move on, since the main point of verse 6 is the same either way. Also, the "rulers and authorities" in verse 10 are debated, so don't let that detail take over the discussion.

4.open: Think of a group you have been part of, like a team, a family or a workplace. What helped it hold together when things got hard?
questions: Paul writes "as a prisoner in the Lord" and still asks them to "walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received" (v. 1). What does it say to you that this appeal comes from a man in chains?
Verses 2 and 3 ask for "humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love." Which of these is hardest for you in a group, and why?

Paul says there is "one body and one Spirit" and "one God and Father of all" (vv. 4, 6). Why might he repeat "one" so many times to people who were struggling to get along? Christians disagree about whether this unity is mainly spiritual or must also show up in one church structure. Where have you seen unity across different churches?
Verse 7 says "to each one of us grace has been given." What is one thing you bring to this group or to your church, even if it feels small?
Pastors and teachers are given "to equip the saints for works of ministry" (v. 12). How does it change things to see ministry as the work of everyone and not only of the leaders?
Paul wants us to stop being "tossed about by the waves" and to grow by "speaking the truth in love" (vv. 14, 15). Where do you find it hard to keep truth and love together?

Verses 22 to 24 talk about putting off the old self and putting on the new. Which part of the old way of life feels most stubborn in you? If you honestly wonder whether change is possible, you can say so here.
Verse 32 says "be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you." What makes forgiving hard, and how does remembering God's forgiveness change that?
4.life: Pick one thing from verses 25 to 32 to practice this week, such as telling the truth, not letting the sun set on your anger, or saying something that builds someone up. If there is a person you need to forgive, take one small step toward that.
4.prayer: Ask God to help your group protect "the unity of the Spirit" (v. 3). Pray for the gifts each person brings and for grace to be kind and forgiving to one another.
4.tip: Verses 26 and 27 and the 'old self' language can leave people feeling guilty or stuck. Remind the group that Paul describes a new self God has already made, and that growth happens together over time. Keep the tone gentle, and do not push anyone to share about anger or forgiveness if they are not ready.

5.open: Who is someone you picked up a habit, a phrase or a way of doing things from without meaning to?
questions: Paul says, "Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children" (v. 1). Why do you think he starts with being loved before he says what to do?
Verse 2 says Christ "gave Himself up for us." What does it look like to love someone that way in ordinary life, at home, at work or in this group?
Verses 3 to 5 put sexual immorality and greed in the same list, and call greed a kind of idolatry. How can money or wanting more become something we serve without noticing?
Verse 8 says, "you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." When you hear that, what comes to mind? If it feels hard to believe about yourself, say so honestly.

In verse 18 Paul says, "Do not get drunk on wine... Instead, be filled with the Spirit." What are the things people reach for to feel lifted or numb, and what does being filled with the Spirit look like instead (vv. 19, 20)?
Verse 21 says, "Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ." Think of a time when giving way to someone felt like care and a time it felt like being controlled. What made the difference?

Christians read verses 22 to 24 differently. Some see a lasting pattern of husbands leading, others see an order of that era moving toward equal partnership, and all agree it never asks anyone to accept abuse. What stands out to you when you read it beside verse 21?
Husbands are told to love "just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her" (v. 25). What does that ask of a husband, and what can any of us, married or not, learn from it about love?
5.life: Pick one person this week and love them in a costly, practical way, giving up some time, comfort or preference for them without making a show of it. Notice what it asks of you.
5.prayer: Thank God that we are his beloved children and that Christ gave himself for us. Ask him to fill you with his Spirit and to shape your closest relationships with the kind of love Christ shows.
5.tip: Verses 22 to 24 may take over the whole evening and can hurt people who have seen control or abuse in a home. Name the disagreement in one line, read verse 21 and verses 25 to 33 alongside it, and make clear that nobody is asked to stay in harm's way. Then steer back to the call to love like Christ.

6.open: When you were a kid, what was the one rule in your house that everyone knew and nobody dared break?
questions: Paul tells children to obey "in the Lord" and tells fathers, "do not provoke your children to wrath" (vv. 1, 4). What do you think healthy honor looks like in a family, from both sides?
Fathers are told to bring children up in "the discipline and instruction of the Lord" (v. 4). What did you receive growing up that helped you, or what do you wish had been different?

Paul speaks to slaves and masters here, and the text does not tell anyone to end slavery. Yet masters are told, "there is no favoritism with Him" (v. 9). How do you read that tension, and how do you think it sounded to people in a Roman household?

Christians have read verses 1 to 9 in different ways, either as a lasting pattern for family and society or as a response to Roman customs that the teaching about one Master was meant to transform. What do you notice in the text that helps you think about it?
Paul says, "our struggle is not against flesh and blood" (v. 12). How might it change the way you handle conflict with a difficult person if you remember that they are not the real enemy?
Paul tells us to "stand firm" and gives each piece of armor, including "the shield of faith" (vv. 14, 16). Which piece do you most need right now, and why?

Paul asks the church to pray for him, "that whenever I open my mouth, words may be given me" (v. 19). He wrote this as "an ambassador in chains" (v. 20). What does it tell you that even Paul needed others to pray for his courage?
Verse 13 says, "having done everything, to stand." If you feel tired or unsure of your faith lately, what would standing look like for you this week, even if it is small?
6.life: Pick one person you will pray for by name every day this week, the way Paul asks for prayer in verses 18 to 20. Tell them you are doing it, if you can.
6.prayer: Ask God for strength "in the Lord and in His mighty power" (v. 10). Pray for each other's families, and for anyone in the group who feels worn down or is struggling to keep standing.
6.tip: Verses 5 to 9 are painful because they were once used to defend slavery. Name that plainly and early, do not rush to defend or dismiss the text, and steer the group toward the one Master who shows no favoritism (v. 9) and toward honest listening.
